A stepwise approach can and should involve introducing different aspects of the functionality employed by compounding workflow technology. For example, while some organizations may introduce gravimetric analysis over a longer period of time, barcode verification should be leveraged for all medications from the beginning. Facilities must also be mindful when placing compounding technology equipment in their cleanrooms. The addition of a scale could represent another potential disrupter of first air within the primary engineering control (PEC). This potential disruption should be documented initially with a visual smoke pattern test and then incorporated into future cleanroom certification studies. Additionally, facilities should be aware of what impact other cleanroom equipment may have on the scale. PECs often vibrate as the motor drives air through the filtration system. At times, this vibration prevents the scale from providing a stable reading. Health systems may need to work with their scale, hood, or compounding workflow solution vendors to secure modifications or replacement of equipment contributing to erratic scale recordings. Health systems should also take advantage of vendor support during the go-live period. Each vendor will have their own scope of service, but all should offer some form of support when rolling out a new compounding workflow solution. Giving preparers the ability to troubleshoot and ask questions in real time, on-site, with “at-elbow” support is recommended, as it provides better experiences for compounding users than remote support offerings. It is important to provide at-elbow support to all shifts of compounders during the initial implementation period, especially on off-hour shifts, when on-site leadership support may be diminished. Special populations Additional consideration should be exercised when compounding for certain populations. An organization’s special populations will likely coincide with those compounds requiring unique skills or preparation types outside of technology. Two of the more common population types with enhanced workflows are also the two often cited to benefit the most from gravimetric technology: oncology and pediatric populations. When preparing oncology medications, it’s vital to take into account the standard use of CSTDs, tubing sets and filters, and medications with limited therapeutic windows. Studies have shown medication retention of 0.1-0.4 mL when using CSTDs, primarily because of the larger dead space in these devices. This loss is crucial with gravimetric analysis given its implication for weighing tolerances. Similar to our recommendations to specify minimum and maximum weight capacities for scales, the authorship team suggests selecting minimum volumes and/or tolerances for preparing medications via CSTDs. Literature suggests volume loss via CSTDs is negligible in volumes greater than 3 mL, which could be used as a conservative minimum volume for gravimetric analysis. Alternatively, or additionally, organizations could also consider raising tolerance on low-volume medications requiring CSTDs to the aforementioned 10%. The bulkiness of tubing and filter sets can also cause complications when users prepare gravimetrically. This is especially true when health systems prime IV bags prior to injecting a medication into them. Preparers must be cognizant of how attached tubing lays on the weighing surface, ensuring it is properly capturing the correct weight of the medication or base. One suggestion is to place a tared basket on the weighing surface, allowing it to contain loose tubing more adequately. Finally, organizations must consider compounding personnel and instrument precision when preparing medications with limited therapeutic windows or specialty components. The order of operations when preparing medications with unique delivery mechanisms (eg, beads) or with supplied components (eg, stabilizers) can also introduce variability. Electronic compounding recipes must be carefully configured to reflect the correct preparation technique. Base fluids, or the final vehicle bags (eg, 0.9% sodium chloride injection, 5% dextrose in water) of an IV piggyback or large-volume bag should also be considered. Compounding leaders must determine the correct time for base adjustments, whether their preparers utilize ACDs or manual manipulation to achieve exact volumes. While this process may vary, the authors have generally seen base adjustment at the beginning of the preparation to be most advantageous to preparing users. Pediatric considerations surround the very small doses often administered in this population. Unfortunately, much of the literature surrounding gravimetric compounding either does not differentiate between populations or specifically excludes pediatric doses when discussing challenges and solutions. Syringe and CSTD dead spaces tend to impact this population to a greater extent, as more of their doses fall in the 0- to 3-mL range. As with oncology, organizations should consider whether alternative tolerance values and/or minimum volumes should be leveraged for these doses. Despite their slight differences, the authorship team recommends utilizing the same standards used for adult doses. As with oncology, organizations should consider whether alternative tolerance values and/or minimum volumes should be leveraged for these doses. Despite their slight differences, the authorship team recommends utilizing the same standards used for adult doses. It is acknowledged that stock solution usage is a common practice to overcome some of these microdoses. One study suggested more preparation errors could be prevented if more accurate equipment were used to prepare these stock solutions. For those reasons, at a minimum, the expert panel recommends gravimetric analysis be used to prepare stock solutions. They also suggest that when possible, gravimetric preparation should be utilized for the subsequent doses resulting from the original stock solution. Future considerations The authorship team acknowledges additional documentation, guidance, and supplementation will be needed to continuously improve nationwide gravimetric compounding adoption, which is currently estimated to have occurred at 7.7% of all US hospitals. The expert panel advocates for additional research and guidance in the areas of ease of implementation, system management and upkeep, and short- and long-term barriers to uptake. The team would also like to advocate for more research on doses compounded gravimetrically for pediatric patients. The authors of this review expect this document will require periodic updates as practice changes and advances in technology dictate modifications. Conclusion The absence of gravimetric analysis integration into compounding workflow technology is a considerable barrier to progress in the accuracy and safety of preparing compounded medications. The evidence and expert opinions documented in this article underscore the potential of gravimetric technology to enhance dose accuracy, reduce errors, and improve patient outcomes when implemented appropriately. As healthcare systems continue to evolve, it is imperative that pharmacy leadership teams consider the integration of gravimetric analysis into their compounding workflows, employing a risk-based approach to determine its application. By embracing this technology and adhering to the guidance outlined in this document, health systems can promote a higher standard of care and safety for their patients.
